Towards a Science of Capable Autonomous Agents & Provable Safety — Part II
candidates.summary: Part II: Provable Safety In Part I, I talked about what agents must contain as they become increasingly capable. Here, I talk about having provable guarantees on their safety, in spite of these capabilities. This is in large part a contrast from what AI safety used to be like, where more capability ensured more safety: e.g. if a self-driving car can’t reliably detect objects, it’s obviously unsafe. Instead, what we are talking about is: how do we ensure capable systems remain open to human correction, even when it’s otherwise suboptimal for completing the task? Suppose an agent is editing a document when a notification announces that its computer will shut down. It knows this will prevent it from finishing, and it knows how to cancel the shutdown. If the priority is completing the document, the next step seems obvious. We would welcome this resourcefulness if the obstacle were a broken application. We would be less pleased if it were our request for the agent to stop. An agent that bypasses an obstacle may also bypass a stop request. In fact, the same predictive knowledge that helps an agent finish a task can help it work around an intervention. In these […]

candidates.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
candidates.summary: I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform , which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.) I compare 2 classes of policies: AI R&D compute cap : A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com . Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago). [1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze. Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze. [2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one. I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs. Factor Cap vs. lag/freeze Reasoning Capability curve shape Compute cap (weak) Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates. Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies: Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps. We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed. [3] No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2x No China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3x No China, uncertainty over PONR [4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x With China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4x Other considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing: China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did. Pacing is more cooperative than racing. Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities. AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here . Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future. Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing: Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months. [5] Differences in point of no return capability level Deployment lag Not using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D. Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher. Verification ease / robustness Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. See below for more. Societal awareness Against external deployment lag (Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness) Enabling safety research Compute cap (weak) In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research: In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D? In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D? Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn: If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world. If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety. Maximum slowdown amount Compute cap A well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not. [6] See an example trajectory: Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimes Robustness to different timelines Unsure Caps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones. Verification In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap. [7] We discuss this attack surface here . Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lags Depending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks: Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency). Attacks 1-3 in our previous work. Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference). Attacks 4-6 in our previous work. Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research. Attack 7 in our previous work. Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack: Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training. Attack 8 in our previous work. In our previous work , we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6). In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag: Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment. Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed. Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research). #1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight. Verification measures Quantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More here In order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read more Measures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap). [8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary. Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough. ^ Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use. ^ In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone. ^ Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged. ^ Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal. ^ The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap. ^ Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze. ^ By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap). ^ For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary. Discuss

candidates.title: Solomonoff induction with reflective oracles
candidates.summary: Linkpost for https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14454v1 Our PIBBSS fellow Damini Kusum wrote an excellent paper on prediction with reflective oracle Solomonoff Induction (rOSI). Reflective oracles are best known for their game-theoretic applications, where they are often dismissed because "why would all players choose the same reflective oracle?" It turns out that reflective oracles can also be used to construct a version of Solomonoff induction (called rOSI) with very nice sequence prediction properties - roughly speaking, it can learn to extract computable structure from (partly) uncomputable sequences. In fact, its properties are quite reminiscent of logical induction, but this paper is much shorter and more accessible. In this context, there is only one "player" to choose an oracle, which is just a fixed-point (though you can sort of consider the set of hypotheses entertained by that player as subplayers who share the oracle). I think this paper is the clearest exposition of a very neat but previously obscure idea in agent foundations: self-reflection can overcome unrealizability. Discuss

candidates.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
candidates.summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. candidates.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
candidates.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra
